institutionName: Institut d'études politiques de Paris (Sciences Po)

questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Career opportunities

questions.question: Please explain: *
Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: It is a valuable addition to my CV, and I have always wanted to live abroad, particularly in Paris.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: As I participated in the introduction programme, I received all the necessary information upon arrival in Paris and had access to contact persons during the first week of my studies who could assist with practical matters related to both living in Paris and the academic aspects of the programme.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: Upon arrival, I received information regarding meeting times and locations. During the introduction week, I participated in a campus tour as well as several guided tours around the city, which helped me settle in quickly and feel comfortable in my new environment.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: Finding off-campus housing in Paris can be both difficult and expensive, and I personally did not secure accommodation until very close to the start of my stay. Many official rental agencies, such as Paris Attitude and PAP, not only charge high agency and service fees but also involve a complicated application process that often requires a guarantor, frequently with a connection to France. In my case, finding accommodation through Airbnb was the best decision, as it involved no agency fees and the process was straightforward.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: I am not certain whether it was possible to live on campus. However, I appreciated the opportunity to find accommodation independently, as it provided greater flexibility in choosing a neighborhood and allowed for a more local experience of living in the city. One of the best decisions I made was to rent an Airbnb in a central and safe area, within walking distance of both the university and many attractions. Although this option was slightly more expensive, it was clearly worth it in terms of convenience, safety, and overall quality of life.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I was not fully satisfied with the housing options provided by the university, which is reflected in my lower rating. However, if you are willing to invest time and effort into finding accommodation independently, it is definitely possible to find a good housing solution.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: To be honest, I found the course registration process quite stressful. Course registration operates on a first-come, first-served basis, and I did not manage to secure all the required courses as a result. I would strongly recommend being fully prepared in advance, with all preferred courses selected and having backup options (plan B, C, and D) ready in case the initial choices are not successful. In addition, I would advise future students to obtain pre-approval for multiple course combinations in advance, especially if they have mandatory courses, as this can help avoid difficulties if they are unable to register for their first-choice courses.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: The registration process was conducted online and operated on a first-come, first-served basis, which made it highly competitive and time-sensitive. And honestly quite stressful.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Information about courses was available through the course catalogue; however, it only contained courses from the previous academic year, which meant that it was not always possible to rely on course availability or schedules not overlapping. That said, Sciences Po’s website was helpful, as it provides a guide to the course registration process, which was useful given that it is not possible to test the registration system in advance and students are introduced to it for the first time when registration opens.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I was not able to register for the courses intended to replace European Politics at my home institution, which required me to follow the course concurrently from home and complicated the course approval and Erasmus process. I strongly recommend having several pre-approved course combinations to avoid being dependent on a single registration outcome.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: I would strongly recommend using Sciences Po’s course registration guide in advance to become familiar with the platform and the registration process. It is also important to review the course catalogue early in order to have a clear overview of possible courses and to be fully prepared on the day of registration. Finally, I advise obtaining pre-approval for several different course options to increase flexibility during registration.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
Overall, I was very satisfied with the academic programme at my host institution. The course selection was diverse and exciting, and I had the opportunity to take courses across different fields, many of which were quite niche and different from the more theory-heavy courses I am used to at the University of Copenhagen. In many classes, it was clear that the instructors were highly passionate about their subjects, which made the learning experience particularly engaging.

Students should be aware, however, that assessment is more continuous than at KU, with grades based on class participation, presentations, midterms, and final papers. This results in a higher workload throughout the semester and can feel somewhat similar to a high-school-style structure, compared to the more exam-focused model at KU. That said, I found the academic level to be largely comparable to KU, if not slightly lower in some cases. There are clear advantages and disadvantages to both systems. One benefit of the continuous assessment model is that the final exam does not necessarily account for 100% of the grade, allowing students to perform well in areas that suit their strengths.

Finally, there was significant variation between courses in terms of assessment methods, which is something future exchange students may want to research in advance if grading structure is important to them.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I found the academic level of the courses to be largely comparable to that of my home institution, the University of Copenhagen, although in some cases slightly lower. The courses were still academically engaging and well structured, with a strong focus on applied learning, discussion, and continuous assessment rather than purely theoretical depth.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: I only had one course taught in a lecture format, while the majority of my courses were conducted as small class teaching with approximately 20–30 students. This made the teaching style more interactive than at UCPH, with a greater emphasis on discussion, participation, and student presentations. Students should also be aware that tests and exams are often handwritten, which feels more old school compared to UCPH, where digital exams are more common. This places a stronger emphasis on memorization and, in some respects, results in slightly lower expectations regarding the level of detail and the amount of written work one is able to produce within the given time

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your second semester. *
What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I found the course The Politics of Urbanism (5 ECTS) to be particularly interesting, both academically and in terms of its practical relevance. The knowledge gained was highly applicable and relatable, and the workload was manageable, as the final grade was primarily based on a research paper and a midterm exam. In addition, the instructor was very passionate about the subject, which further enhanced the overall learning experience.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Grocery shopping was generally more expensive than I had expected, particularly when it came to vegetables. Otherwise, I found prices to be fairly similar to those in Denmark. On the positive side, many museums and cultural institutions are free for EU citizens under the age of 26, which helps reduce cultural expenses. There are also affordable lunch options available through CROUS, the university canteen system. Personally, I chose to eat out quite often, as Paris offers a wide range of excellent cafés and restaurants. Overall, I believe it is largely a matter of prioritization, and it is certainly possible to live more cheaply than I did.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I did not actively participate in non-academic activities such as clubs or sports during my exchange, and therefore cannot fully assess these opportunities.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: While I did not participate extensively myself, there appeared to be a wide range of cultural, athletic, and social activities available through numerous student organizations. These included both academic and non-academic associations, offering many opportunities for students who wish to engage in activities outside the classroom.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I would highly recommend participating in events organized by the Danish Church in Paris, as they offer a welcoming community for Danish students and provide a nice sense of familiarity while living abroad. The events are generally very cozy and well attended, and I met many good friends through these activities. Additionally, I would strongly recommend taking advantage of the free museum access for EU citizens under 26, as it allows you to explore a wide range of cultural institutions without feeling pressured to spend an entire day at each one.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Museums and simply exploring the city on foot were how I spent most of my time. Paris is a city where you can easily spend hours wandering through different neighborhoods and discovering new places. In addition, there are endless opportunities to visit excellent cafés and restaurants, making it hard to know where to begin. Paris truly offers something for everyone.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: I found it relatively easy to adjust to the local culture. I lived in the 5th arrondissement, which is central but also quite local and calm, and this made it easy to settle in and establish everyday routines, such as finding local shops, public transport, and the route to and from the university. There is some truth to the perception of a language barrier, as at times I encountered locals who were not always willing or comfortable speaking English, or not particularly patient with attempts to speak French. However, this was generally manageable and should not discourage future exchange students.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Socializing with local students can take some effort, as French students are often primarily present in French-taught courses and may already have established social circles. However, the French students I interacted with were generally very friendly and willing to help, for example by offering advice or tips. I also found that there tended to be more French students in larger courses, such as Comparative Politics (10 ECTS), which provided better opportunities for interaction.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: The language barrier was one of the main challenges, and I found that the general approach to service can feel more reserved compared to Denmark. Paris can also be intense and overstimulating at times, as there is constant activity and less informal interaction with strangers. In addition, there is a strong culture of queuing - whether for restaurants, museums, or other attractions - so patience is sometimes required.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: I really appreciated the strong culture of enjoying everyday life. There is a vibrant dining culture, with people going out to eat regardless of the day of the week, and the city is constantly alive with new events and experiences. As a result, it feels like you never truly finish exploring Paris.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Start looking for housing early. I would strongly recommend Airbnb, as it can be a flexible and relatively straightforward option compared to many traditional rental agencies in Paris.

Do not be intimidated by the academic level. I was initially concerned, as Sciences Po is often described as an elite university, but students from UCPH are generally very well prepared academically. Be aware, however, that the workload can be higher than in Denmark. Even so, make sure to experience the city—this is what you will remember in the long run, and you do not need to be perfect to pass.

Prepare thoroughly for course registration. Familiarize yourself with the registration process in advance, have backup course options ready, and obtain pre-approval for multiple course combinations if possible.

Extra tip: Apply for scholarships and grants! A small investment of time in this can really pay off!

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Teaching at the host institution is relatively traditional, with a strong emphasis on memorization and handwritten exams. Whether this suits a student’s learning style is largely a matter of personal preference, as there are both advantages and disadvantages to this approach. Additionally, attendance requirements are quite strict, as students are generally not allowed to miss more than two classes per course without documentation before failing the course. Overall, the French academic system can feel more demanding and structured than some other exchange destinations, and students should be prepared for a less flexible and more academically rigorous environment.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer:
One of the most rewarding parts of my exchange was meeting so many great people, both Danish and international students. I also really enjoyed experiencing everyday life in another country and building a routine in a new city. My biggest advice is to really enjoy it — time goes by incredibly fast. The semester is only 12 weeks, and suddenly it’s over.

On a personal level, it was a huge confidence boost to complete a full semester abroad. Sciences Po has a reputation for being academically demanding and highly selective, which honestly felt a bit intimidating before I left. Going through the semester and succeeding there was therefore very rewarding and showed me that I could easily keep up in a new academic environment.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: The biggest challenge was the workload, which at times was quite intense and required long days at the library. I also found it challenging to strike the right balance between academic responsibilities and making the most of living in Paris. At times, this came with a bit of guilt—either for studying instead of exploring the city, or for being out enjoying the city when I felt I should be studying.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: Reading back my answers, some of this may sound a bit negative or overwhelming, but that is not the overall picture I want to leave. My exchange was an incredibly rewarding experience—academically, socially, and personally. If you are in doubt about going, my advice is simply: do it. You learn so much, gain countless new experiences, and come home without really missing out on life back home. Once you return, everyday life continues as if you were never gone, and suddenly the whole exchange almost feels like a dream.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
